What neither this file nor claims.json can see (#195): test/test_claims.py holds SEED_IDS <= the registry's ids, and the registry against the claim-marked tests in both directions, and neither direction can detect a claim the source makes that nobody wrote down -- an inventory checked against itself cannot find an entry missing from both. That is #120's weakness with an instance: claims.json held 32 records and none about the exchange matrix K, while [JEngine, v2, §6] says recomputing [r]^(0) has more merit for K because of the contractions at the shell quartet level, and §1 characterises Wang et al.'s [24] f-type K splitting. limits.claim: exact_given_inputs on jengine/table1 (FLOPs): no recovered set of inputs reproduces all 40 printed cells. The cut IS recovered (plan/recovery.py, two-ended nearest fill per direction, which also gives all 40 of Table 3); the sieve's inputs are not. Refused under the rules-only doctrine (#108): a per-cell fitted seed order is not admitted as a recovered input.
limits.mechanism: Table 1 is post-sieve, and the sieve's output depends on its seed order: an order of a batch's targets, up to 969! of them at L = 16, one batch. [JEngine, v2, §4.1] says the order moves FLOPs and node count by up to ~2%, and that the authors did not optimise it; they do not state the order they used. So the order is an unpublished input with no rule to recover it from, and the printed cells sit inside its spread. Also unpublished, and searched below: which other direction a re-parented child takes, how far the upward sweep deletes, and whether the walk is breadth- or depth-first.
limits.evidence: Every search below uses the recovered cut and the counting conventions #10 fixed (1/2/3 FLOPs per node by r_d; fundamentals with m > 0 are intermediates). (1) The literal sieve seeded in hermite_targets order: 9/40 exact, (7,3) (7,6) (7,9) (8,6) (8,9) (9,6) (9,9) (10,9) (11,9). (2) The literal sieve over plan/recovery.py's 26 structured seed orders (hermite_targets and its reverse; |r| ascending or descending, then the components in each of the 6 axis orders, all ascending or all descending): best 17/40 ('|r| asc, then xzy desc'). (3) A scratch variant of the sieve, not kept in the repo, over those 26 orders x 7 re-expansion choices (smallest r_d', largest r_d', xyz, zyx, smallest r_d' ties to z, cyclic successor, cyclic predecessor) x 2 sweeps (every orphaned node, or only i and its parents upward) x breadth- or depth-first x [r-1d] or [r-2d] enqueued first: 1456 configurations, best 17/40 Table 1 together with 29/40 Table 2. (4) Random seed orders, each sieved twice (smallest- and largest-r_d' re-expansion): 6000 runs (3000 orders) at (7,1) and at (8,1) reach the printed pair in 3578 and 460 of them, so those cells ARE seed-order effects; 600 runs (300 orders) at (16,1) never reach it (best FLOPs 5666 against the printed 5633; the hermite order gives 5644), so the paper's order there is in the tail, and no rule this search knows names it. Bounded at that point on purpose: the remaining space is the factorial order space itself, and searching it for each cell would be a per-cell fit. (5) #108, THE WIDENED FAMILY: plan/recovery.py's seed_orders(widened=True), the 26 above plus 32 rules each with a stated rationale (FLOPs of the target's MILD closure asc/desc; out-degree of its MILD parents asc/desc; sieve-greedy, by how many of its parents already pass Alg. 3's test, desc/asc; direction-major by batch_direction in the 6 axis orders; max-then-mid component in the 4 sign combinations, '+max/-mid' being the predecessor tree's base rule), each with hermite and reversed-hermite tie-breaks: 58 orders, literal sieve, recovered cut. Table 3 stays 40/40 under every one. Best Table 1: 33/40, one order only, '+max/-mid, ties reversed' (max component ascending, middle descending, then reversed hermite position); the same order is the unique best on Table 2 (38/40). Its 7 Table 1 misses are (13,3) (14,3) (15,1) (15,3) (16,1) (16,3) (16,6), every one OVER the printed FLOPs (+0.11% to +0.32%), and its 2 Table 2 misses (15,3) (16,1) are both UNDER the printed intermediates: the residual has one sign per table, the same trade test_plan_sieve.py's anchors show for the hermite order, which points at a choice inside the sieve (re-expansion), not at the seed order. That order was picked by its score from 58 named rules, so 33 is itself a selection over rules; it is still a rule applied to every cell, and it does not reach 40. THE DECISION (#108): RULES ONLY. exact_given_inputs records rules the paper's numbers were produced by, the same for every cell; a per-cell fitted order is not admitted, not even under a separately named rule. Reasons: (a) the predecessor tree's per-cell orders show a fit exists (all 40 cells of Tables 1-3, 29 cells needing no transposition, the rest 1-5 swaps off its own '+max/-mid' rule, found by a beam search scored against the Article's numbers), but those values do not transfer (a different cut recovery and seed-order family), and a fit shows only that some order reproduces a number, which is evidence of nothing about the method; (b) the one-sign residual above says a fit here would absorb a systematic difference in the sieve into per-cell inputs, so the fitted record would be wrong about what it records. The 7 cells stand at their printed values.

What is recorded is what that pass is and is not: a choice the board makes, cell by cell, by a bounded search over explicit per-batch seed orders -- not a recovery of the paper's inputs, which stay unpublished, and not a claim that the paper used these orders.
limits.mechanism: The printed cells are post-sieve, and the sieve's output depends on its seed order, which [JEngine, v2, §4.1] says moves FLOPs and node count by up to ~2%, was not optimised, and is not stated (the jengine/table1 exact_given_inputs record above has the full argument). A rule over r and L cannot be shown to be the paper's draw, and #108's rules-only doctrine refuses a per-cell fit on the literal board; that refusal is unchanged. The searched board is not bound by it: it scores the plan the generator could take, and since #172 that plan's seed order is a per-batch permutation climbed from the 58 rules. So a pass here says the printed cells are reachable -- at or under, in all three tables at once -- inside a declared, bounded order space, by a selection rule declared before the board was read (#171, unchanged). It says nothing about which order the authors drew: 22 cells land on the printed triple exactly, and the other 18 come in under it, which the printed values could not if they were this search's output. The residual #171 recorded -- 8 cells of Table 1, worst +0.89%, 6 of them unreachable in the 58-rule space and 2, (14, 1) and (14, 3), the selection rule's price -- was a bound of the space searched, as the 26-order residual before it was: it is kept below as previous_residual, the old space's numbers.

Per batch the frontier of every order evaluated; per cut order_search.product of the batches' frontiers; over the feasible cuts the frontier (60 points over the 40 cells). Every 58-rule plan on a feasible cut is evaluated, so the climbed frontier weakly dominates the 58-rule space there (test_plan_search.py). SELECTION (#171), unchanged: feasible if max targets <= the cell's minimax + 1; the Pareto frontier over (max_intermediates, FLOPs); the point minimising intermediates / intermediates_min + flops / flops_min, ties to fewer intermediates. RESULT: Table 1 0/40 over, Table 2 0/40, Table 3 0/40; in 14 cells (strictly_dominates_58_rule_selection) the selected plan is better on both axes or on one and equal on the other than #171's selection from the 58 rules, and in the other 26 it is the same point. CHOSEN AFTER READING THE BOARD, said plainly: the starts and the budget. Climbing every distinct rule order with a budget of 200 per run, on the 8 previous residual cells, passed 6 and left (14, 1) and (15, 1) over Table 1, each with a frontier point at or under all three that the rule passes over; the frontier starts with a budget of 2000 are cheaper and are the space recorded. The selection rule and at_or_under were not touched. HISTORY of the residual: the first search (cut only, minimax tolerance 0) 30, 13, 0 cells over and a worst margin of +7.50% at (15, 9) Table 2; the 26-order search 21, 3, 0 and +2.04%; #168's 58-order lexicographic search 9, 0, 0 and +0.89%; #171's frontier and selection rule 8, 0, 0 and +0.89%; #172 0, 0, 0. NOT SEARCHED: per-direction cuts, orders more than 2000 examined neighbours from a climbed start, the sieve's re-expansion choice and sweep (the jengine/table1 record above searched those against exact_given_inputs and stopped at 17/40), and no-sieve.

limits.claim: jengine/batching-crosses-our-ridge, #114's own claim: does batching move OUR [p|q] kernels across OUR cards' ridge? Answered on sm_86 only. gfx1200's answer is ABSENT (could not measure), and no answer here says anything about [JEngine, v2, Fig. 7]'s A100 result, which stands as the paper's and is not ours to dispute.
limits.mechanism: (1) THE RIDGE IS THE CARD'S. A verdict is intensity against peak fp64 over bandwidth, and our measured ridges -- 0.65 FLOP/B on sm_86 and 1.49 on gfx1200, ACHIEVABLE rates from this box's probes (data/measured/ceilings.json, #109), not datasheet peaks -- are each that card's; Fig. 7's A100 ridge is a different number, from a different card, and no comparison is drawn with it. Consumer fp64 is cut hard on both of our cards, so a class may be compute-bound ALREADY AT ONE BATCH here, and on sm_86 three of the four subgrid L are: that is a statement about the card, not about batching, and not a contradiction of the paper. (2) THE AMD ANSWER IS ABSENT. gfx1200 has no counter rows (measured_store.UNMEASURED, #112), and since #140 the refusal is FINAL: rocprofv3 1.1.0 now loads in this container, but rocprofiler-sdk defines no fp64 instruction counter for gfx12 (SQ_INSTS_VALU_*_F64 exist for CDNA only), so it gives no measured FLOP count and hence no measured intensity; and its GL2C byte counters read 0 on this box, so it gives no bytes either. Could not measure is recorded as such, never as 'never crossed'. (3) WHAT THE INTENSITY SEES. The bytes are ncu's DRAM traffic (32-byte sectors) on ONE input, #53's wide-T (2048 x 128), in a counter run that serialises and replays each kernel; a batch whose working set stays in L2 hardly touches DRAM, so a split cell's kernel intensities spread over orders of magnitude, and another input or cache could move a verdict near the ridge. The verdict is a threshold, not a margin: L = 13 at 1 batch is compute-bound at 0.96 FLOP/B against 0.65. (4) WHICH CLASSES. SUBGRID's L are 7, 10, 13 and 16, with b in {1, 3, 6, 9, 12}: L = 10 is Fig. 7's [5|5], L = 13 and 16 bracket its [7|7], and [6|6] (L = 12) is not measured (#112 measured the compile cost and declined it). (5) THE PER-KERNEL VARIANT AT ONE BATCH IS THE CELL: a one-batch partition is one kernel, so the two variants can differ only past 1 batch; on sm_86 they do not differ at all. (6) WHAT THE FLOPS COUNT (#116). The numerator is every fp64 instruction the kernel issues (ncu's dadd + dmul + 2 dfma), the Boys evaluation included, whereas [JEngine, v2, Table 1]'s FLOPs exclude the Boys function; an intensity here is not Table 1's FLOPs over any byte count, and the counter run, which serialises and replays each kernel, is not the timed run (counter_ns is never a timing). (7) THE CEILINGS ARE ACHIEVABLE RATES, at the clock the card ran them (#141): the ridges come from this box's probes, not datasheets. The #116 assumption -- that gfx1200's published fp64 figure (0.801 TFLOPS) could count RDNA4's fp32 dual-issue -- is RETIRED, not assumed: a GRBM_GUI_ACTIVE cycle count puts the probe at 127.95 flop per GPU cycle, the single-issue 2 fp64 FMA lanes per CU per clock (32 CUs x 2 x 2 = 128; the probe is plain v_fma_f64, and VOPD dual-issue has no f64 form), so its sanity bound is now per clock (published.gfx1200.per_clock). The recorded 0.446 TFLOPS is ~111% of the 0.4006 TFLOPS rated-boost figure because the card ran the probe at a counted ~3.49 GHz, above its 3130 MHz rated boost: the 1.49 FLOP/B ridge is the card at that clock, and a clock-limited run of the same card would have a lower one. gfx1200 has no verdict to move.
limits.evidence: felizjueves.ridge over data/measured/roofline.json (124 kernel rows, 20 cells, sm_86, ncu 2025.3.1.0, recorded by #112 behind the card gate), recomputed by measure/measure_ridge.py::test_batching_crosses_our_ridge_on_sm_86_and_gfx1200_could_not_measure. sm_86, both variants identical: L = 7, 10, 13 compute-bound already at 1 batch (300, 3.54, 0.96 FLOP/B), compute-bound at every higher count too; L = 16 memory-bound at 1 batch (0.40 FLOP/B) and crossed at 3 (cell 1.52 FLOP/B, smallest kernel 1.46), compute-bound at 6, 9, 12 as well. gfx1200: could not measure. CROSS-READ AGAINST #60 (9 batches do not suffice on either card): on sm_86 every kernel of every 9-batch cell is compute-bound, so the roofline does NOT explain #60's verdict as kernels still memory-bound at 9 -- it contradicts that reading. sm_86's 9 fails #60 only on SPILL (12 spills less at L = 13 and 16) while 12 is slower than 9 at every L on both inputs; the roofline agrees with the clock there, since there is no ridge left to cross at 9. On gfx1200, where 12 wins on near-T at L = 16, the roofline can say nothing: no rows.

limits.claim: jengine/ket-sort-key-beats-the-global-max on our cards (#147): the per-record product key I_q * max_q |D_q| against one global max|D|, same tau, molecule and batch count, both arms in one gated session per card. The declared expectation -- the global key is worse -- is CONTRADICTED on sm_86 and on gfx1200; two of the eight cells are below what this box can resolve.
limits.mechanism: (1) THE SCREEN. I_pair (ao/pairs.py) is pair-factor-free: a ket's Gaussian pair factor and dressing live in its dressed D_q, so its distance decay reaches the screen only through Dmax. A global Dmax erases it, and on every input here the global key skips NO (bra, ket) record pair, at either tau -- the screen's work goes the expected way, by the whole of the product's skips. (2) THE ORDER. The global key changes the ket order too (by I_q alone, i.e. by exponent and pair momentum) and that order is not free: on the two-H2 chain at tau = 1e-10 the product arm skips 560 of 8100 pairs and is still slower than the global arm, which skips none, by 21% on sm_86 and 9% on gfx1200 -- the two arms differ in ket order and keys only. At tau = 1e-3 (2790 skipped) the skips win. Why the product order costs time is NOT measured here; a candidate is the per-ket work of the device Boys (emit/_c.py's Kummer loop, whose length grows with T), grouped by exponent under the I_q order and interleaved under the product order, so lanes diverge more. (3) THE NOISE FLOOR is #60's: the larger of the two arms' IQRs over 31 timed builds. On sm_86 the H2O/cc-pVDZ builds are bimodal (near 8.5 and near 10 ms, IQRs 1.3-1.6 ms), so its two cc-pVDZ cells are the weakest: tau = 1e-3 reads BETTER by 1.57 ms over a 1.36 ms floor, tau = 1e-10 UNRESOLVED. On gfx1200 the cc-pVDZ tau = 1e-3 arms are equal to 3 us (UNRESOLVED) while tau = 1e-10 reads BETTER by 1.69 ms over a 0.25 ms floor. The chain cells resolve on both cards (IQRs under 13 us). (4) THE INPUTS: the chain is two H2, not #88's four, because the four-H2 sweep asks the card's fj_boys for T up to 1289, past its witnessed [0, 500] and its overflow near 700; the four-H2 chain's skip counts (66060 and 36072 of 104976 for the product, 0 for the global key) are the oracle's only.

limits.claim: A `Launch` IR and a `LaunchCost` model for the whole-molecule J of [JEngine, v2, §6]: DELIBERATELY ABSENT (#148, milestone 6's description (c), decided before any of its code). No IR represents the launch sequence, no model predicts what a whole build costs, and so nothing here ranks one launch plan above another or says the plan's order is the BEST one. J resident on the card across SCF iterations is out of scope by the same decision.
limits.mechanism: Milestone 6 makes the plan a VALUE and nothing else: `launch.LaunchPlan` (#138) says which [p|q] kernels run, over which index records, in which order. Each consumer checks the plan directly instead of going through a fourth representation of it: the launch oracle `launch.walk` (#142, pure Python, equal to the host's screened sweep to 0), the staged interpreted driver `ao/staged.py` (#143), and the device `main()` that `test/plan_driver.py` writes from a plan for the card (#144). That driver lives under `test/`, not `src/felizjueves/emit/`: the generator still emits kernels, not launch code. A `LaunchCost` would model a build with only the clock to score it against. The one per-kernel model this repo has, `lower.KernelCost`, already mis-ranks the measured rows it is scored against (data/measured/limits.json, #54 and #60). So the build is MEASURED (data/measured/builds.json, #146) and never predicted. The only ordering question put to the clock is #147's single A/B of two sort keys, and its declared expectation was contradicted on both cards (the jengine/ket-sort-key-beats-the-global-max record above). Residency stops at one build. Every timed build zeroes its J_p buffers, launches, and reads them back. The uploads happen once per process, outside the clock. Eq. 20's back-transform and the J_ab scatter run host-side in Python. Moving those to the device is milestone 7's subject. (Milestone 7 did: the E transform, the pre-contraction and the scatter are generated kernels since #152-#157, run on both cards on this same test-side driver; see the three records below. Nothing in builds.json times them, and this record's decision is unchanged.)

limits.claim: The screen's granularity, compared with the predecessor `jgen`: `jgen` maps one warp per SHELL PAIR and screens per shell pair, while this repo maps one warp per PRIMITIVE-PAIR RECORD and screens per record (#138, milestone 6's description (b)). This is a READING of [JEngine, v2, Alg. 1], not a defect on either side. Every n_pairs, n_skipped, skip fraction and launch-list length this repo records counts record pairs. None of them is comparable one for one with a shell-pair screen's count.
limits.mechanism: Alg. 1 reads a per-index Ip / Iq and does not say what an index is. This repo's bound, `I_pair` (ao/pairs.py), is pair-factor-free and proved per primitive-pair record (test/test_ao_pairs.py, over randomised geometry). The kernel contract maps one warp per bra record, by index. So the launch lists are record lists grouped by class. Where the IR did NOT reach, the kernels worked around it and the work-around is recorded here: (1) no nested `Inline` (#149's one-level rule), so the E block is composed at build time from one axis builder rather than by inlining the axis fragment three times; (2) `Fn` has no ABS or MAX, so DQ writes |x| and max_q with LT and SUB; (3) #149's hygiene refuses a host array named like a fragment's scalar bind, so JAB's exponent array is `zeta_ab`, not the contract's `zeta`; (4) an array extent must be a scalar `Param`, so DQ gains `n_pair` and JAB `n_rows`, which nothing reads, and which the emitter casts to (void) because hipcc's -Wunused-parameter otherwise fails #92's warning filter (#156).

So the form that was built for [p|q] reaches E unchanged, and widening the IR took vocabulary only (the `Factor`s 1/2zeta, PA, PB and `Fn.EXP`). Nothing structural was added. The four work-arounds above are the IR's edges as this milestone met them. None is a defect in a kernel. None changes a bit of the result, and each is spelled in its module's docstring.
